question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Provisional number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported in Statistics Korea's monthly Population Trends release.
target.caveats: The July 2026 monthly figure is provisional and its first release is expected after the 2026-08-23 information cutoff, so no published target value should be assumed. Working interpretation: live births by occurrence date under KOSTAT's vital-statistics definition; coverage and treatment of foreign

candidates.hypothesis: July live births follow a recurring seasonal slice of the recent monthly birth level; if provisional births in early 2026 are above or below their year-earlier counterparts, July 2026 should move in the same direction, subject to July-specific seasonality and reporting changes.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly provisional live births for July in 2019-2025, all available 2025 monthly values, and any 2026 monthly values published before 2026-08-23 (likely through May or June), with release dates. If unavailable, annual births plus monthly shares for July.
search_hints: Statistics Korea monthly population trends live births July

candidates.hypothesis: Monthly civil birth registrations track statistical live births with a registration lag; July 2026 registrations or partial registration counts can constrain the occurrence-based July estimate after adjusting for lag and completeness.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly birth registrations from family-relations registration or resident-registration administrative statistics for 2024-2026, especially June-July 2026 if available by the cutoff; release dates and lag patterns versus KOSTAT births.
search_hints: resident registration births South Korea monthly

candidates.hypothesis: Marriages lead first births by roughly a gestation-plus-conception interval, so marriage registrations in late 2025 and early 2026 should provide a directional signal for July 2026 births; the transfer assumes Korea's birth-marriage linkage remains strong.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly marriage registrations for 2024, 2025, and available 2026 months from KOSTAT, with emphasis on September-December 2025 and any correlation or lag relationship to monthly births.

candidates.hypothesis: Delivery-related medical claims or hospital delivery cases approximate the number of births, with coverage differences for foreign residents and timing lags between delivery and claim; recent claim volumes can indicate July 2026 delivery activity.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly counts of childbirth- or delivery-related health-insurance claims or hospital delivery cases for 2024-2026, especially any data through June or July 2026; definitions, coverage, and claim lag.

candidates.hypothesis: Applications for universal birth-related vouchers or child benefits are filed shortly after birth and can proxy live births, though eligibility and application timing introduce coverage and lag errors.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly application counts for First Meeting Voucher, parent benefit, or similar birth-linked programs for 2024-2026, especially July 2026 applications or the latest available months, with eligibility scope.
search_hints: First Meeting Voucher applications monthly births Korea

candidates.hypothesis: Annual births can be decomposed into age-specific fertility rates times the female population of childbearing ages; this structural route constrains whether a monthly July figure is plausible relative to the 2025-2026 fertile population and fertility level.
candidates.data_to_find: Latest age-specific fertility rates for 2024 or 2025, female population by five-year age group for 2025-2026, and annual birth totals or projections from KOSTAT. Monthly July seasonality may require an additional share assumption.

candidates.hypothesis: New birth incentives, marriage tax or housing policies, and lingering COVID-era timing shifts can create level changes in monthly births; identifying measurable policy start dates and affected cohorts helps judge whether extrapolated 2025-2026 trends over- or under-state July 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Dates and scope of major 2024-2026 birth or marriage incentives, monthly births around prior policy changes, and evidence on COVID-related birth timing in Korea; avoid treating announced targets as outcomes.

candidates.hypothesis: Published annual 2026 birth forecasts can be converted to a July estimate using historical July shares; the route constrains the annual level but depends on the forecast's definition and the stability of monthly seasonality.
candidates.data_to_find: Annual 2026 live-birth forecasts for South Korea published before 2026-08-23 from KOSTAT, Bank of Korea, research institutes, or international bodies, with forecast date and assumptions; historical July share of annual births.

methods.rationale: Alternative d1 route: infer Jan-Jun 2025 live births from same-vintage Jan-Jul 2025 cumulative (p20) minus July 2025 (p16), then apply the Jan-Jun 2026 level (p13) times the July 2025/Jan-Jun 2025 seasonal ratio. This avoids using p14's revised Jan-Jun 2025 baseline but is sensitive to p20/p16 vintage consistency. It shares p16 with m1 and is not independent; the two methods bracket the H1 baseline uncertainty.

assessment.note: p15 is just the arithmetic difference of p13 and p14 (H1 2026 up roughly 15% on H1 2025), so this is one measurement channel, not three confirmations. All three trace to a single Wikipedia table built from KOSTAT releases (snapshot 2026-07-08). Caveat: a Jan-Jun 2026 cumulative is slightly ahead of KOSTAT's ~2-month publication lag for that snapshot, so the row may be a running/partly provisional aggregate; it is used as the level-shift signal with that caveat, and m2 checks it against a same-release baseline.

p20 minus p16 implies Jan-Jun 2025 = 126,001 (first-report vintage, Sept 2025 article), while p14 states 127,184 for the same period (2026-07-08 vintage): a ~0.9% revision/vintage gap, not a definitional contradiction. Both baselines are carried forward separately rather than blended silently: m1 uses p14, m2 uses the internally consistent p20-p16.

Same July 2025 KOSTAT release: July 2025 births 21,803, the highest July since 2021's 22,364 (p19), consistent with the 147,804 Jan-Jul cumulative (p20). Establishes that July 2025 was already a seasonally strong, above-trend month, which is the base that July 2026 must beat.

Within the same release, July 2025 TFR 0.80 (joint-highest month of 2025) and CBR 5.0 confirm July as a seasonally high month. Not independent of p16 but supports treating July 2025 as a valid carrier of July seasonality rather than an outlier month.

p1 (independent news report on KOSTAT data) says the 2026 Jan-May cumulative is the largest Jan-May since 2019's 134,433, i.e. below 134,433 but well above 2020-2025. That is consistent with p13's Jan-Jun total once a normal June month is removed, and therefore cross-checks the ~15% H1 surge from a second, one-step-removed source.

Annual KOSTAT series 2022-2025 (249,186 → 230,028 → 238,343 → 254,457) documents the 2024-2025 rebound (+6.8% in 2025) that makes a further 2026 increase directionally plausible. p2 also supplies the July-share benchmark (July 2025 / 2025 annual ≈ 8.6%) used as a plausibility check on any July level, not as an independent input.

NHI delivery claimants 235k vs KOSTAT 238k live births in 2024 (98.6%), and total delivery rate 0.70 vs TFR 0.75, move together. This sets a ~1.4% coverage gap so a claims-based count would need a small upward bridge — but no 2026 claims vintage exists in the evidence, so this channel cannot produce a July 2026 level and is kept only as a coverage bridge.

Live births / pregnancy-voucher expected-delivery persons is stable at 81.9-84.9% across 2021-2024 (82.4% in 2024). The gap is administrative composition (non-live-birth outcomes, coverage of foreign residents), not random noise, so it is a usable bridge factor — but no 2026 voucher cohort mapped to July 2026 deliveries is available.

Voucher expected-delivery persons rose 7.2% in 2025 (8.3% in Jan-Apr 2025) while Jan-Apr 2025 live births rose 7.6%, showing birth-adjacent administrative flows track statistical births within a few points and slightly understate them. These are 2025-vs-2024 quantities, so they inform the direction of the rebound but cannot be transferred to July 2026 without a 2026 voucher vintage.

Restored from round 1: July 2025 yoy growth 5.9% (p18) versus Jan-Jul 2025 cumulative growth 7.2% (p21). In 2025 the July month-specific yoy ran at roughly 0.8x the year-to-date rate, which is the empirical basis for the damping factor a1 in m3 rather than an invented coefficient.

methods.rationale: d1 route, later-vintage baseline: July 2026 is treated as July 2025's level (p16, first-reported monthly Population Trends value) carried forward by the change in H1 cumulative live births (p13 versus p14). This transfers the 2026 level shift to July while preserving July's own seasonal position (July 2025 ran slightly above its H1 monthly average). Failure modes: p13 may be a running aggregate revised later (its period label sits ahead of KOSTAT's publication lag for the snapshot date), so the ~15% H1 shift could be overstated or understated; if part of the H1 2026 gain is births pulled forward from H2, m1 overstates July. Shares its only signal with m2 and m3, so those are not independent confirmations.

a1.role: dimensionless damping of the H1 2026 yoy growth rate when applied to the single month of July 2026, calibrated from the 2025 July-versus-cumulative growth gap

methods.rationale: Guards the extrapolation against over-fitting a single H1 surge to one month. It applies the H1 2026 growth implied by p13/p14 to July 2025 (p16), attenuated by a1, which is grounded in the observed 2025 pattern where the July yoy (p18) ran below the year-to-date growth (p21) and in the fact that July 2025 was an unusually strong July base. Failure modes: if the 2026 rebound is a persistent level shift rather than a fading or timing-driven surge, a1 will be too low; the damping factor is a judgement parameter and carries the widest uncertainty of the three routes. Shares p13/p14/p16 with m1, so it is not independent evidence, only a different transfer assumption.

assumptions.name: Damping factor: July 2026 yoy birth growth relative to H1 2026 yoy growth
assumptions.rationale: Empirical analogue from the same series: in 2025 the July month-specific yoy birth growth was 5.9% (p18) while the Jan-Jul cumulative growth was 7.2% (p21), i.e. the July rate ran at about 0.8x the year-to-date rate. In addition, July 2025 was itself a strong month relative to its own H1 average (p16 vs p14/p20), so the July 2026 comparison base is unusually high and a full pass-through of the ~15% H1 2026 surge is unlikely. The range 0.5-1.2 spans material deceleration (part of the H1 surge being timing pull-forward, which would fade by July) through no damping or slight amplification (if the rebound is a broad marriage-driven level shift that keeps accelerating). It is a dimensionless factor on an observed change, not a level.
assumptions.applies_when: July 2026 month-specific yoy growth can reasonably differ from the H1 2026 yoy growth, and the difference is expected to resemble the 2025 pattern where the single-month yoy ran below the cumulative rate.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that July 2026 delivery activity grew at or above the H1 2026 pace (for example July 2026 voucher expected-delivery persons or NHI delivery claims well above the H1 rate), or evidence that the H1 2026 surge was concentrated in January-March and had already faded by June.

methods.rationale: Guards the extrapolation against over-fitting a single H1 surge to one month. kept.applies_when: July 2026 month-specific yoy growth can reasonably differ from the H1 2026 yoy growth, and the difference is expected to resemble the 2025 pattern where the single-month yoy ran below the cumulative rate.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that July 2026 delivery activity grew at or above the H1 2026 pace (for example July 2026 voucher expected-delivery persons or NHI delivery claims well above the H1 rate), or evidence that the H1 2026 surge was concentrated in January-March and had already faded by June.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
